subtitulo: Must have, might have, can't have at the office
descripcion: At B2 the modal perfect of deduction (must have, might have, can't have) is learned in single, clear sentences. Building an extended reasoning chain across several sentences (C1) isn't the target yet — getting one deduction right is enough.

filas: It might have been a mistake.
He can't have known about it.

ejemplos.texto: She must have left already — the lights are off.
It might have been a scheduling error.
He can't have known about it, or he would have said something.

notas: Must have expresses near certainty based on evidence, not a guess out of nowhere.
Can't have is the negative equivalent of must have, not couldn't have.
The participle after these modals is always the past participle, regardless of the tense of the situation.

es.en: Spanish expresses deduction with deber de + infinitive (debe de haber salido), close in logic to English must have. For a dismissed possibility Spanish uses no puede haber…, which maps well onto can't have; the typical error is using the negative of must instead (mustn't have).
es.es: El español expresa deducción con «deber de» + infinitivo («debe de haber salido»), con una lógica cercana a «must have». Para una posibilidad descartada usa «no puede haber…», que se corresponde bien con «can't have»; el error típico es usar en cambio la negación de «must» («mustn't have»).

de.en: German builds the same structure (Er muss gegangen sein; er kann es nicht gewusst haben), so the logic transfers well. The trap is the negative: German speakers often use mustn't have for a dismissed possibility, where English says can't have.
de.de: Das Deutsche bildet dieselbe Struktur («Er muss gegangen sein; er kann es nicht gewusst haben»), daher lässt sich die Logik gut übertragen. Die Falle liegt in der Verneinung: Deutschsprachige verwenden bei einer ausgeschlossenen Möglichkeit oft «mustn't have», wo Englisch «can't have» verlangt.

it.en: Italian has close equivalents (deve essere uscito – he must have gone out; non può essere uscito – he can't have gone out), so the logic transfers well. The Italian futuro anteriore (sarà uscito) is a separate source of error, producing he will have gone out.
it.it: L'italiano ha equivalenti vicini («deve essere uscito» – «he must have gone out»; «non può essere uscito» – «he can't have gone out»), quindi la logica si trasferisce bene. Il futuro anteriore italiano («sarà uscito») è però un'altra fonte di errore e può produrre «he will have gone out».

fr.en: French puts the modal itself in the perfect (il a dû sortir), which leads to the calque he has had to go out instead of he must have gone out. For the negative, il ne peut pas être sorti corresponds well to he can't have gone out.
fr.fr: Le français met le modal lui-même au passé composé («il a dû sortir»), ce qui conduit au calque «he has had to go out» au lieu de «he must have gone out». Pour la négation, «il ne peut pas être sorti» correspond bien à «he can't have gone out».

pt.en: Portuguese has the same order as English (deve ter saído – he must have gone out; não pode ter saído – he can't have gone out). Portuguese speakers therefore handle modals of deduction with very little interference.
pt.pt: O português tem a mesma ordem que o inglês («deve ter saído» – «he must have gone out»; «não pode ter saído» – «he can't have gone out»). Por isso, falantes de português lidam com modals of deduction com pouca interferência.

errores: Using couldn't have instead of can't have to rule something out.
Using the base form instead of the participle: must have leave instead of must have left.
Confusing might have and must have when the evidence actually supports a stronger conclusion.

es: *puede que* rendered with *can* for possibility: *He can be at home* instead of *He may be* or *might be at home*.
de: Using *had to* for a past deduction, from *musste*: *He had to be tired* instead of *He must have been tired*.
it: *può darsi che* rendered with *can* for possibility: *He can be at home* instead of *He may be* or *might be at home*.
fr: *il se peut que* rendered with *can* for possibility: *He can be at home* instead of *He may be* or *might be at home*.
pt: *pode ser que* rendered with *can* for possibility: *He can be at home* instead of *He may be* or *might be at home*.

redemittel.expresion: There's no way she could have…

traducciones.es: No hay forma de que ella haya…
traducciones.it: Non è possibile che lei abbia…
traducciones.pt: Não é possível que ela tenha…

redemittel.funcion: matches the modal to the actual certainty

traducciones.de: Wie sicher bin ich mir eigentlich?
traducciones.fr: Mais à quel point en suis-je sûr ?

mision.consigna: Your application at an office has disappeared. Work out what must have happened.

microtareas.texto: Five guesses about why there's a *delay*.
Rewrite them from most to least certain.
Record 90 seconds: what *must have* happened to your file?

autochequeo: Is the participle correct after the modal verb?
Is can't have used to rule something out, not couldn't have?
Does the chosen modal match the actual level of certainty?
Have I used at least two different modals of deduction?
Is the sentence based on real evidence, not a random guess?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on modals of deduction. Check the participle form after each modal and the choice between must, might, could and can't have based on the actual evidence in the text. Do not rewrite the text.
